The natural measure is the close's position in the high-low range, `close / (high - low)`, which is a ratio so it is comparable across coins of different price units. I'll start with the simplest form — the close's position in the day's range, averaged over a few days.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so I need a range measure that is comparable across coins and with the sign flipped at the outermost layer. The simplest level form would be log(high/low), averaged over a few days, with `-1` on the outside. I'll start there.

The idea says the range is bearish, so I'll keep that sign and try to sharpen the measure: a log range is scale-free and the ratio is already a monotone transform, so the next thing worth changing is the window length. I'll test the same formula with a 10-day mean.

The direction is as the idea says: coins with wide daily ranges do underperform afterwards. Widening the window from 5 to 10 days and switching from a mean to a median both made it slightly worse, so a short 5-day mean is the version I keep.

The idea is about a coin's dollar volume being low relative to its own recent range, so the plainest measure is where today's `quote_volume` sits inside its own 20-day range: a low position means the coin is under-volume, which the idea says should be bullish. I'll start with that simplest form.

The rank IC is −0.029 and the incremental IC is −0.0160 with the same sign in every period, so on this history coins that sit low in their own dollar-volume range keep underperforming — the idea as stated looks wrong here. Before concluding, I'll check whether the measure is just noisy: a 20-day rank of a single day can jump around, so I'll average it over the last 5 days first.

Averaging over 5 days barely moves the number (−0.0172 vs −0.0160), so the instability of a single day is not the issue. One more genuinely different reading of "within its own recent range": a 60-day range instead of a 20-day one, which should be less noisy and less driven by one-off volume spikes.

What I found: measuring a coin's dollar volume against its own recent range, as a rank position, gives a consistent but negative incremental IC (−0.0160, t = −5.8) with the same sign in all three sub-periods (2022H2 −0.0295, 2023 −0.0196, 2024 −0.0055). So on this history the idea does not hold: coins that sit low in their own dollar-volume range keep underperforming rather than bouncing, and the effect is stable across periods. I keep the direction the idea states — low position in the range, higher factor — and report honestly that it fails here.

Measuring "far" against the coin's own typical range instead of its own high-low range destroys the signal (−0.0004), so the plain ratio is the better measure of the idea. The raw rank IC is negative (−0.0169), meaning the raw shape is partly a reversal/volatility effect that the style removal keeps; what survives is the part that is genuinely new information.
